question:
A feature request I have to implement is written as loose prose, and the product owner and I keep reading it differently. How should the team pin down, together with the domain experts and before any code is written, what the feature must do, so that it cannot be misread?

Answer with a list of guidelines. After each guideline, cite the source it comes from: the path of the SWEBOK file if you have it, otherwise a verbatim quote of at least 8 words from the passage, in the form (source: ...).
answer:
# Summary

When a feature is described in ambiguous prose, the team should work with domain experts before coding begins to express requirements in precise, unambiguous, and testable language—using structured formats, concrete scenarios, and collaborative review to ensure all stakeholders interpret the feature the same way.

# Guidelines

- Convene software engineers, business domain experts, and QA professionals **before any production design or construction work** [SWEBOK excerpt 2ef4734028e44ae6e102] demonstrate the feature is correctly implemented. (source: /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Requirements_ Foundations and Engineering Practices/Requirements Engineering_ Elicitation, Analysis, and Specification/Requirements Specification and Validation Techniques/Test-Driven Development and Acceptance Testing/Acceptance Criteria-Based Requirements Specification.md)

- Use BDD scenario language in the form "Given \<context\>, when \<stimulus\>, then \<outcome\>" to describe each concrete situation the feature must handle, since test-case language is precise where natural language is inherently ambiguous. (source: /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Requirements_ Foundations and Engineering Practices/Requirements Engineering_ Elicitation, Analysis, and Specification/Requirements Specification and Validation Techniques/Test-Driven Development and Requirements Specification/Acceptance Criteria and BDD Scenarios for Banking Systems.md)

- Aim for a comprehensive set of scenarios covering all relevant situations, including edge cases such as disabled cards or insufficient funds, so that no behaviour is left undefined. (source: /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Requirements_ Foundations and Engineering Practices/Requirements Engineering_ Elicitation, Analysis, and Specification/Requirements Specification and Validation Techniques/Test-Driven Development and Requirements Specification/Test Cases, Requirements, and Behavior-Driven Development.md)

- Write each requirement so that it is **unambiguous** (interpretable in only one way), **testable** (quantified so compliance can be clearly demonstrated), and **atomic** (representing a single decision). (source: /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Requirements_ Foundations and Engineering Practices/Requirements Engineering_ Elicitation, Analysis, and Specification/Requirements Analysis and Refinement/Software Requirements Properties and Quality Criteria.md)

- Conduct a requirements review in which clients and users verify their needs are completely and accurately represented, while other engineers check the document for clarity, consistency, and conformity to standards. (source: /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Requirements Validation and Management/Requirements Validation Methods and Techniques.md)

- Where the specification cannot be directly reviewed, build a prototype that concretely demonstrates important aspects, exposing engineers' assumptions and giving stakeholders useful feedback on misinterpretations. (source: /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Requirements Validation and Management/Prototyping for Requirements Validation and Feedback.md)

- Consider using structured natural language formats such as the actor-action format ("When \<event\>, \<actor\> shall \<action\> unless \<condition\>") to increase precision and reduce ambiguity beyond plain prose. (source: /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Requirements_ Foundations and Engineering Practices/Requirements Engineering_ Elicitation, Analysis, and Specification/Requirements Specification and Validation Techniques/Requirement Specification Formats and Structures/Actor-Action Format in Requirements Statements.md)

- Use formal or semiformal modeling languages (e.g., UML, SysML, Z) when higher precision is needed, since [SWEBOK excerpt 72ac55dd2bf5f751ed75] and the less likely engineers are to misinterpret it. (source: /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Requirements_ Foundations and Engineering Practices/Requirements Engineering_ Elicitation, Analysis, and Specification/Behavioral Models and Requirements Documentation/Behavioral Modeling Approaches and Formality Levels/Formal Modeling Methods for Requirements Specification.md)

- When stakeholders keep reading the requirement differently, apply the 5-whys technique—[SWEBOK excerpt 1fe68f3f10ebf9873c97] underlying problem rather than an assumed solution. (source: /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Requirements_ Foundations and Engineering Practices/Requirements Engineering_ Elicitation, Analysis, and Specification/Requirements Analysis and Refinement/Software Requirements Properties and Quality Criteria.md)

- If conflicts persist between the product owner and domain experts, negotiate a consensus resolution among the stakeholders rather than letting the engineer make a unilateral decision, and ensure the resolution is traceable back to the customer. (source: /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Requirements_ Foundations and Engineering Practices/Requirements Engineering_ Elicitation, Analysis, and Specification/Requirements Engineering_ Viability, Verification, and Stakeholder Management/Managing Conflicting Requirements in Software Engineering.md)

- Document supplemental attributes alongside each requirement—such as rationale, source, acceptance criteria, and dependencies—so engineers can better interpret and manage what the feature must do. (source: /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Requirements_ Foundations and Engineering Practices/Requirements Engineering_ Elicitation, Analysis, and Specification/Behavioral Models and Requirements Documentation/Formal Requirements Models and Additional Attributes.md)
